newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian accused of murder in U.S. to stand trial.
newsitem.headline: Italian accused of murder in U.S. to stand trial.

text.p: An Italian suspected of killing a tax inspector in Florida was committed for trial in southern Italy on Tuesday on a charge of premeditated murder.
Pietro Venezia, who has been in detention in Italy since his arrest on an international warrant in 1994, was ordered by a committal judge in his home town of Taranto to stand trial from October 2.

Italy's Justice Ministry agreed in 1995 to a request by the state of Florida for Venezia's extradition but Italy's Constitutional Court blocked the move in a ruling last June because of the use of capital punishment in the state.

Venezia, who is in his 40s, is accused of killing of tax inspector David Bonham in Miami in 1993. He is alleged to have shot Bonham dead at Bonham's house for freezing his bank account in a probe into a $41,000 tax evasion.
The defendant told Tuesday's preliminary hearing that the gun went off accidentally.
His lawyer, Cataldo Fornari, said he would ask for his client to be granted house arrest pending the trial.
"Venezia has confessed, although he obviously maintains that he did not kill Bonham voluntarily," Fornari told reporters.

The U.S. government had provided assurances that prosecutors would not press for Venezia to face the electric chair if convicted of first degree murder, an option available under Florida state law. Italy does not have the death penalty.

Italy's 1983 extradition treaty with the United States contains a clause allowing extradition in return for sufficient guarantees that the death penalty will not be imposed or carried out in the relevant case.

The Constitutional Court ruled that the provisions were unconstitutional and said capital punishment was incompatible with Italian constitutional safeguards of human rights, including the right to life.
